ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
ACCPPDE101.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
ACCPPDE101.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
ACCPPDE101.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

MCCMEDI111.name: Introduction to Film & Media
MCCMEDI111.description2: Introduces film and media as systems of meaning and cultural production. Examines how images, narratives and technologies shape perception, identity and power; covers film storytelling, representation and genres; and develops critical engagement skills.
MCCMEDI111.profile: Introduces how moving images create meaning through cinematography, editing, sound, mise-en-scène, narrative and performance. Film history connects early cinema, Expressionism, montage, Hollywood and New Waves to feminist and postcolonial interpretation. Broader media topics include television, digital platforms, representation and spectatorship. An independent analytical or creative-analytical project combines close analysis, theory, scholarly research and, where chosen, original media work.
MCCMEDI111.topics: Film form and meaning; Cinematography, editing and sound; Mise-en-scène, narrative and performance; Early cinema; German Expressionism and Soviet montage; Classical Hollywood and European New Waves; Feminist film theory; Postcolonial media; Blockbusters; Television and digital platforms; Representation and spectatorship; Media convergence
MCCMEDI111.methods: Close film and media analysis; Historical and cultural contextualization; Application of feminist and postcolonial film theory; Independent analytical or creative-analytical media research

MCCCOMM111.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
MCCCOMM111.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
MCCCOMM111.profile: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
MCCCOMM111.topics: Greek and Roman rhetoric; Deliberative, forensic and epideictic discourse; Logos, ethos and pathos; Invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery; Argumentation and fallacies; Tropes and schemes; Stasis and enthymemes; Persuasive speech; Narrative and storytelling; Immersive educational communication
MCCCOMM111.methods: Rhetorical text analysis; Stasis analysis; Argument invention and arrangement; Stylistic analysis and composition; Structured debate; Persuasive speechwriting and delivery; Educational storytelling design

GOSSOCI111.name: Introduction to Sociology
GOSSOCI111.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
GOSSOCI111.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
GOSSOCI111.topics: Sociological imagination and knowledge; Social structure and socialization; Classical social theory; Colonialism and the formation of sociology; Solidarity and modernity; Identity, belonging and othering; Groups and social networks; Capital, class and mobility; Race and gender inequality; Global inequality and migration; Education and labour-market inequality
GOSSOCI111.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
BENGATE102.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
BENGATE102.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
BENGATE102.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis

HCBPSYC111.name: Social Psychology
HCBPSYC111.description2: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
HCBPSYC111.profile: Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations. Social cognition, the self, influence and persuasion lead into group processes, prejudice, aggression, prosocial behaviour, attraction and close relationships. Students critically examine empirical research, synthesize findings from journal articles, formulate theory-guided questions and design a feasible study. The final project proposes research rather than conducting an empirical investigation.
HCBPSYC111.topics: Social cognition and person perception; The self and self-motives; Social influence; Persuasion, attitudes and behaviour; Group processes; Prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination; Prejudice reduction; Interpersonal aggression; Prosocial behaviour; Interpersonal attraction and close relationships
HCBPSYC111.methods: Critical appraisal of empirical social-psychology research; Literature synthesis; Theory-guided hypothesis formulation; Research design for a proposed social-psychology study

MCCCOMM213.name: Rhetoric in Action
MCCCOMM213.description2: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
MCCCOMM213.profile: Applies rhetoric through community-engaged work with local primary-school children. Students develop their own public-speaking, debating and storytelling skills, then design and iteratively refine age-appropriate teaching activities with school partners. On-site coaching and a final public-speaking event connect rhetorical education to civic participation and confidence. Structured reflection examines reciprocity, cultural sensitivity, personal development and the practical challenges of community-engaged teaching.
MCCCOMM213.topics: Public work of rhetoric; Community-engaged learning and reciprocity; Public speaking and debate; Storytelling; Children's rhetorical confidence and civic participation; Rhetorical teaching and coaching; Cultural sensitivity; Collaboration with community partners; Experiential and reflective learning
MCCCOMM213.methods: Public-speaking and debate coaching; Storytelling exercises; Iterative design and revision of teaching materials; Practice-based rhetorical instruction; Gibbs reflective-cycle analysis; Public-speaking event design and evaluation

BENLEAD112.name: Leadership Communication
BENLEAD112.description2: This course blends theory with practice from both fiction and the real world, helping you develop essential leadership skills. Learn how to inspire teams, sharpen your communication, take ethical decisions, and lead with confidence.
BENLEAD112.profile: Studies leadership communication through leadership theory, persuasion and practical rhetorical work. Students compare contemporary leadership approaches and examine emotional intelligence, gender, culture and ethics. Literary characters, film and speeches provide material for analyzing effective and ineffective leadership. Students interview a real leader, analyze the leader's communication challenge in an advisory report, and develop a public address presenting their own ethical leadership vision.
BENLEAD112.topics: Leadership models and approaches; Transformational, authentic and adaptive leadership; Servant leadership and followership; Emotional intelligence; Leadership ethics; Gender and culture in leadership; Persuasion and organizational communication; Leadership in literature and film; Storytelling and public speaking; Personal leadership vision
BENLEAD112.methods: Leadership-theory application; Literary and film-based leadership analysis; Professional interviewing and note collection; Leadership-discourse analysis; Communication-advisory report development; Rhetorical speechwriting and storytelling

DISDATA111.name: Introduction to Data Science
DISDATA111.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
DISDATA111.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
DISDATA111.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
DISDATA111.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis

BENGATE101.name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
BENGATE101.description2: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.
BENGATE101.profile: Introduces entrepreneurship and core business functions through the development of a startup concept. Students use design thinking to discover customer needs, define a problem, generate and prototype solutions, and construct value propositions and business models. Marketing, finance, operations, human resources and funding inform a coherent business plan and investor pitch. Entrepreneurial cases and a startup simulation examine decision-making, early growth and business lifecycles, with attention to societal impact and sustainability.
BENGATE101.topics: Entrepreneurial mindset and pathways; Business environments, ownership and competition; Customer needs; Value propositions; Business models; Marketing and sales; Finance and accounting; Venture funding; Operations and human resources; Competitive positioning; Startup growth and business lifecycles; Sustainability and societal impact
BENGATE101.methods: Design thinking; Customer-needs discovery; Ideation and prototyping; Value Proposition Canvas; Business Model Canvas; Business planning; SWOT and risk assessment; Startup simulation

MCCMEDI112.name: Media Archaeology
MCCMEDI112.description2: Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.
MCCMEDI112.profile: Examines media technologies as material and cultural artifacts, moving from early print through optical projection, telegraphy, typewriters and analogue sound to digital networks. Students apply recurring theoretical perspectives to how physical properties and infrastructures shape communication, knowledge and memory. Hands-on object, listening and recording exercises connect historical evidence to lived experience. Independent research analyzes a selected media object or phenomenon using appropriate media-archaeological methods.
MCCMEDI112.topics: Media materiality and memory; Print culture; Optics and projection; Telegraphy and infrastructure; Mechanical inscription; Broadcasting and sound fidelity; Portable analogue media; Cassette revival; Computing and networks; Media geology; Technological obsolescence; Mechanical reproduction and aura
MCCMEDI112.methods: Media-archaeological artifact analysis; Historical and technical media comparison; Facsimile and manuscript-print analysis; Media-protocol investigation; Comparative listening and sound-fidelity analysis; Analogue recording exercises; Historical media-object research

GOSSOCI214.name: Modern Sociology
GOSSOCI214.description2: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
GOSSOCI214.profile: Examines twentieth-century and contemporary social theory alongside critical accounts of modernity, colonialism and disciplinary exclusion. Functionalism, critical theory, Black feminist thought, phenomenology, symbolic interactionism and Bourdieu's work are read with postcolonial, decolonial and Indigenous perspectives. Students compare theories and apply them to empirical cases, including visual material. An individual research paper develops a theoretically grounded interpretation of a selected social phenomenon.
GOSSOCI214.topics: Modernity and Eurocentrism; Functionalism; Frankfurt School critical theory; Black feminist thought and intersectionality; Social construction of reality; Symbolic interactionism; Stigma and othering; Social space, capital and art; Coloniality and postcolonialism; Decolonial and Indigenous sociology; Gender and power
GOSSOCI214.methods: Close reading of social theory; Comparative theoretical analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Visual sociological analysis; Literature-based sociological research

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
GOSSOCI212.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
GOSSOCI212.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
GOSSOCI212.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation

MCCCOMM211.name: Style & Meaning
MCCCOMM211.description2: Explores how linguistic choices inform meaning and interpretation in literary and non-fiction contexts. Introduces theoretical frameworks for close reading and addresses power dynamics, obligation, uncertainty and ideological undertones in language.
MCCCOMM211.profile: Studies how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts but also in nonfiction. Students connect linguistic description to interpretation across grammar, discourse and cognition. Stylistic frameworks address foregrounding, dialogue, narration, modality, transitivity, deixis, schemas, construal and text worlds. Frequent analysis exercises lead to an original, research-supported stylistic analysis of a selected text.
MCCCOMM211.topics: Foregrounding and deviation; Morphology, syntax and lexical semantics; Register and cohesion; Dialogue and turn-taking; Cooperative principle; Speech and thought presentation; Modality and point of view; Transitivity and ideology; Narrative urgency; Figure and ground; Deixis and deictic shift; Schemas, scripts and prototypes; Cognitive grammar and construal; Text-world theory; Negation and lacuna
MCCCOMM211.methods: Linguistic stylistic analysis; Close textual analysis; Discourse and conversation analysis; Speech and thought presentation analysis; Modality and transitivity analysis; Deictic and cognitive-grammar analysis; Text-world analysis; Framework-based interpretation supported by retrievable textual evidence

MCCMEDI211.name: From T.V. to TikTok
MCCMEDI211.description2: Explores how media shape attitudes and provide answers through examples from TV and TikTok. Examines messages that teach fear, pity, admiration and allyship.
MCCMEDI211.profile: Examines American social history and everyday life from the mid-twentieth century through contemporary media. Storytelling, power and representation connect television, film and digital forms to conformity, identity and imagined futures. Students analyze 1950s media, compare dominant portrayals with Indigenous self-representation, and investigate disability representation. Futures-oriented projects create a speculative television-episode proposal and imagine possibilities that center disabled people.
MCCMEDI211.topics: Media storytelling and power; American everyday life; 1950s television and conformity; Science fiction and social anxieties; Media futures and marginalization; Indigenous representation and self-representation; Disability stereotypes and visibility; Authentic voice and cultural agency; Future foresight and inclusive scenarios
MCCMEDI211.methods: Historical analysis of primary media sources; Comparative representation analysis; Future-foresight scenario development; Theory-based speculative narrative design; Disability-centered futures inquiry

DISARIN111.name: AI Ethics
DISARIN111.description2: Explores philosophical foundations and implications of AI. Examines the history of AI, ethical issues like interpretability, bias and alignment, debates about AI consciousness and implications for human nature.
DISARIN111.profile: Examines AI through ethical theory and psychological accounts of human behaviour and interaction. Ethical debates address fairness, privacy, responsibility, alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Psychological perspectives consider development, clinical care, social and organizational relationships, forensic applications and cognitive neuroscience. Students synthesize literature and apply ethical frameworks in an analytical psychology project and a research-grounded podcast, with a creative communication component.
DISARIN111.topics: Algorithmic fairness and bias; Privacy and surveillance; Responsibility and accountability; Human-value alignment; Moral status of AI; Existential risk and democratic implications; Trust and agency in human-AI interaction; AI in clinical care; Child development and AI; Social and organizational effects of AI; AI in forensic psychology; Cognitive and socioemotional development; AI consciousness and sentience
DISARIN111.methods: Ethical-framework application; Philosophical argument evaluation; Psychological-literature synthesis; Theory-based analysis of AI applications; Research podcast scripting, recording and editing

MCCMEDI311.name: Media & Race
MCCMEDI311.description2: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
MCCMEDI311.profile: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.
MCCMEDI311.topics: Racial construction and whiteness; Media, power and representation; Leisure, tourism and racial identity; Crime, punishment and the racialized body; Asian-American exclusion; Japanese-American incarceration; Childhood and youth; Marginalized and Indigenous storytelling; Racial extremism and propaganda; Alienation and community; Food, environment and cultural nourishment; Afrofuturism and Indigenous futurisms
MCCMEDI311.methods: Participant observation; Archival primary-source research; Historical media analysis; Documentary podcast research, scripting and audio production; Photo/Voice photography and audio narrative; Cross-cultural interpretive reflection

MCCCOMM311.name: Persuasive Communication
MCCCOMM311.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
MCCCOMM311.profile: Examines contemporary persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis, then applies it in community-engaged work. Students study coactive persuasion, framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Projects with the Delta Climate Centre and Vlissingen municipality develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles. An individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools through literature review, field research diaries and reflective analysis of their use.
MCCCOMM311.topics: Persuasion models and psychology; Ethics of persuasion; Coactive persuasion; Verbal and nonverbal communication; Message framing; Argumentation; Cognitive shortcuts and nudging; Science and sustainability communication; Circular lifestyles; Community-engaged communication
MCCCOMM311.methods: Persuasive-message design; Communication consulting and implementation; Literature review; Qualitative research diaries; Action research; Reflective case-study analysis; Gibbs reflective cycle

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.description2: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
GOSSOCI311.profile: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.
GOSSOCI311.topics: Civil society; Social trust and social capital; Hegemony; Critical theory; Public spheres, digital publics and counterpublics; Solidarity and civil repair; Civil sphere; Social movements and intersectionality; Migrant solidarity; Civil society under authoritarianism; Decolonial critique; Public sociology
GOSSOCI311.methods: Comparative social-theory analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Document and secondary-source analysis; Structured reflection on civil-society engagement or observation; Sociological research design

HCBPSYC315.name: Youth Resilience to Extremism
HCBPSYC315.description2: Interdisciplinary course combining psychology and other social sciences in which students will have an opportunity to participate in an actual international research project and develop evidence-based materials for youth leaders and educators aimed at strengthening young people’s resilience to radicalization by promoting democratic school culture, emotionally supportive learning environments, empathy, civic engagement, and mental well-being.
HCBPSYC315.profile: Examines youth radicalization and educational prevention through psychology, education, sociology, political science and peace education. Models of radicalization and adolescent risk and protective factors lead into inclusive school climates, belonging, social-emotional learning, dialogue, media literacy and civic agency. Students translate primary research into teacher-training materials and a youth toolkit for an international school project, then revise the resources using feedback from intended recipients.
HCBPSYC315.topics: Radicalization, violent extremism and terrorism; Developmental and psychosocial pathways; Risk and protective factors; School climate and belonging; Identity and peer influence; Social-emotional learning and well-being; Empathy and perspective-taking; Conflict resolution and intercultural dialogue; Mental-health literacy and referral; Digital literacy and misinformation; Youth leadership and democratic participation; Counter- and alternative narratives
HCBPSYC315.methods: Primary-research synthesis; Intervention-evidence appraisal; Case and classroom-scenario analysis; Inclusive educational-resource design; Alternative-narrative development; Recipient-feedback collection and iterative revision; Ethical appraisal of prevention tools

MCCMEDI212.name: Media & the Environment
MCCMEDI212.description2: Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture. Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.
MCCMEDI212.profile: Examines how visual, audiovisual, sound and digital media shape understanding of ecological problems and human-nonhuman relations. Environmental-humanities concepts guide close analysis of images, narratives and aesthetic strategies across cultural and historical contexts. Students investigate how scientific knowledge, risk and lived experience become representations that influence ethics, public debate and sustainability. A final analytical paper or media-based project develops an argument grounded in course theory.
MCCMEDI212.topics: Environmental representation; Anthropocene; Animal representation and human-nonhuman relations; Deep time and ecological temporality; Biocentrism and environmental justice; Contested ideas of nature; Indigenous and postcolonial media; Ecological risk and scientific knowledge; Environmental affect and perception; Agency, scale and responsibility; Sustainability discourse
MCCMEDI212.methods: Close film, image and sound analysis; Comparative analysis of media forms and representational strategies; Ecocritical interpretation; Theory-based analytical or creative media inquiry

MCCMEDI312.name: The Documentary
MCCMEDI312.description2: Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study.
MCCMEDI312.profile: Studies documentary history, modes and styles alongside practical documentary production. Students analyze nonfiction representation in historical, social, ethical and aesthetic contexts, from early and Soviet filmmaking through direct cinema and contemporary forms. Topics include propaganda, advocacy, ethnography, history, nature, audio and interactive documentary. Production workshops guide a short film through preproduction, filming and postproduction, with reflection on interviewing and representational choices.
MCCMEDI312.topics: Documentary definition, modes and ethics; Early documentary and city symphonies; Soviet filmmaking; European documentary traditions; Direct cinema and cinéma vérité; Audio and public-affairs documentary; Propaganda and advocacy; Historical and ethnographic documentary; Nature documentary; Mockumentary; Interactive and autobiographical documentary; Documentary aesthetics
MCCMEDI312.methods: Critical documentary analysis; Historical and contextual film comparison; Documentary research and interviewing; Script, storyboard and shot-list development; Preproduction planning; Documentary filming and postproduction; Reflective evaluation of production practice

MCCCOMM212.name: Communicating the Climate Crisis
MCCCOMM212.description2: Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.

BENENTR311.name: Market Research
BENENTR311.description2: See how companies figure out what customers love and what they don’t. You’ll plan and carry out real research, analyze what you find, and share your results. Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business ideas. Ready to turn curiosity into career skills? Perfect for future marketers, analysts, or entrepreneurs.

DISGATE101.name: Introduction to Programming
DISGATE101.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
DISGATE101.profile: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
DISGATE101.topics: Python language fundamentals; Strings and input/output; Branching and loops; Functions; Tuples, lists, sets and dictionaries; Aliasing and cloning; Recursion; Exceptions and assertions; Object-oriented programming; Inheritance; Computational problem-solving
DISGATE101.methods: Structured programming in Python; Object-oriented programming; Recursive problem-solving; Program tracing; Testing and debugging; Exception handling

DISDATA212.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision
DISDATA212.description2: Covers processing and analysis of image data, including feature detection and tracking. Discusses applications in medicine, self‑driving vehicles, gaming, robotics and traffic management.
DISDATA212.profile: Examines how digital images are represented, processed and interpreted to recognize structures and objects. Spatial and spectral representations, colour and image statistics support filtering, segmentation, curve and feature detection, tracking and object classification. Students use Python and OpenCV to implement image-processing techniques, investigate spectral representations, and build a recognition pipeline whose performance is benchmarked on previously unseen images.
DISDATA212.topics: Spatial and spectral image representations; Cameras and calibration; Colour models and quantization; Image histograms; Point operators; Linear and nonlinear filters; Edges and contours; Mathematical morphology; Image segmentation; Curve and corner detection; Feature detection and tracking; Object localization and classification; Recognition performance
DISDATA212.methods: Python and OpenCV programming; Image filtering; Histogram and point transformations; Morphological image processing; Hough transform; Image segmentation; Feature matching and tracking; Recognition-pipeline design; Benchmark evaluation on unseen images

DISGATE102.name: Mathematical Methods
DISGATE102.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
DISGATE102.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
DISGATE102.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
DISGATE102.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis

BENBUSI211.name: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
BENBUSI211.description2: This course includes a multi-faceted exploration of AI’s business, managerial, economic and related societal implications. Designed for students with a strong interest in AI, it requires no prior technical background.
BENBUSI211.profile: Examines AI's business, economic and societal implications without requiring a technical background. AI foundations and limitations lead into applications across enterprise functions and industries, labour-market change, productivity, innovation, market structure and inequality. Governance, corporate responsibility, regulation and future scenarios connect technological developments to institutional choices. Students analyze business cases and competing scholarly arguments, then investigate a country's AI readiness, workforce, regulation and industrial policy.
BENBUSI211.topics: AI capabilities and limitations; AI in business functions and industries; Agentic AI; Market structure and business models; Automation and augmentation; Labour markets and productivity; Innovation and economic growth; Inequality; Techno-economic paradigms and economic narratives; AI ethics and societal impacts; Corporate governance and AI regulation; National AI readiness and industrial policy; Future AI scenarios
BENBUSI211.methods: Business-case analysis; Comparative analysis of economic arguments; Evidence-based policy argumentation; Comparative country AI-readiness analysis

DISDATA311.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
DISDATA311.description2: Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent developments in large language and image generation models.
DISDATA311.profile: Develops neural-network theory and practical implementation in Python, Keras and TensorFlow. Students build and train simple networks before studying multilayer architectures, backpropagation, regularization and model evaluation. Later work applies deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects construct predictors for tabular data and investigate an independently chosen image- or text-based prediction problem, with experimental results reported in a paper.
DISDATA311.topics: Perceptrons and ADALINE; Multilayer neural networks; Gradient descent and backpropagation; Bias-variance trade-off and regularization; Computation graphs; Network architectures and interpretation; Computer vision; Time-series learning; Text classification and generation; Transformers and large language models; Feature engineering; Predictive performance
DISDATA311.methods: Python programming; Keras and TensorFlow network implementation; Gradient-descent training; Backpropagation implementation; Neural-network performance evaluation; Tabular prediction; Image classification; Text classification and generation; Deep-learning experimental design

BENLEAD311.name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership
BENLEAD311.description2: This course offers Liberal Arts and Sciences students a deep dive into the psychological, social, and structural dynamics that shape workplaces. Through interactive case discussions, simulations, and real-world insights, students develop critical skills in motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and culture. By synthesizing research and applying theory to practice, participants gain the tools to navigate and influence diverse organizational environments effectively.
BENLEAD311.profile: Examines organizational behaviour at individual, group and organizational levels. Topics connect personality, perception, emotions and motivation to teams, leadership, power, conflict, structure, culture and change. Students design research plans for organizational cases and conduct a brief systematic literature review using PRISMA reporting tools. Workshops develop literature searching, study selection, source appraisal and synthesis, linking organizational-psychology evidence to practical questions and recommendations.
BENLEAD311.topics: Diversity, equity and inclusion; Job attitudes and satisfaction; Emotions, stress and workplace health; Personality and individual differences; Perception and decision-making; Motivation; Group behaviour and work teams; Human resource systems; Communication, conflict and negotiation; Leadership, power and politics; Organizational structure; Organizational culture and change
BENLEAD311.methods: Organizational case analysis; Research design and hypothesis formulation; Systematic literature review; PRISMA flow diagrams and checklists; Database searching and study screening; Source-quality appraisal and evidence synthesis

BENLEAD312.name: Negotiation & Strategic Thinking
BENLEAD312.description2: How do you get to yes? In this course you will learn how to craft persuasive arguments, deploy the right language, negotiate more effectively, and influence decisions with confidence—whether in business, leadership, or life.
BENLEAD312.profile: Develops negotiation as an analytical practice and interpersonal skill. Students learn interest-based bargaining, BATNA and ZOPA, value creation, framing, concessions and strategies for handling power, emotions and difficult counterparts. Social-psychological and communication perspectives connect negotiation to trust, ethics, culture and relationships. Frequent simulations and narrative analysis lead to an annotated negotiation film and the design, teaching and evaluation of a negotiation scenario grounded in Delta Climate Center themes.
BENLEAD312.topics: Interests versus positions; BATNA and ZOPA; Mutual gains and objective criteria; Dual-concern model; Anchoring, framing and concessions; Trade-offs and logrolling; Cognitive biases and influence; Power and emotions; Trust, reputation and ethics; Cross-cultural and organizational negotiation; Negotiation implementation and withdrawal; Stakeholder interests
BENLEAD312.methods: BATNA and ZOPA analysis; Stakeholder-interest mapping; Interest-based negotiation; Negotiation simulations; Narrative and film analysis of bargaining; Negotiation-scene scripting and annotation; Scenario design and reflective evaluation

BENLEAD211.name: Psychology of Leading Under Pressure
BENLEAD211.description2: What does it take to lead effectively through pressure, conflict, and diversity? Explore how emotion, identity, belonging, and inclusion shape leadership, teamwork, and performance. Design and conduct an original empirical study while building career-ready skills in research design, data analysis, teamwork, ethical decision-making, and scientific communication.
BENLEAD211.profile: Examines how emotion regulation, emotional intelligence, emotional expression and suppression, emotional labor, belonging, identity safety and psychological safety shape leadership and social interaction under conflict, exclusion and interpersonal uncertainty. It emphasises inclusive leadership and ethnic, cultural, sexual and gender minority experiences, with digital emotion regulation as a further strand. Students conduct a supervised quantitative survey project: formulating theory-driven hypotheses, selecting established psychological measures, designing and piloting a Qualtrics survey, recruiting participants ethically, collecting original data and preparing a clean dataset. Individual work applies descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlations, group comparisons and introductory multiple regression in SPSS or RStudio, and interprets findings and limitations in empirical reports and evidence-based leadership recommendations.
BENLEAD211.topics: Emotion regulation strategies; Emotional intelligence; Emotional expression and suppression; Emotional labor; Inclusive leadership; Belonging and identity safety; Psychological safety; Ethnic, cultural, sexual and gender minority experiences; Digital emotion regulation; Psychological measurement, reliability and validity; Ethical survey research in diverse populations; Interpretation and limitations of quantitative evidence; Evidence-based leadership recommendations
BENLEAD211.methods: Theory-driven hypothesis formulation; Quantitative survey research; Established psychological measure selection and evaluation; Qualtrics survey construction and piloting; Ethical participant recruitment and original data collection; Codebook development, reverse coding and scale scoring; Data cleaning and missing-data documentation; Descriptive statistics; Reliability analysis; Correlation analysis; Group comparisons; Introductory multiple regression in SPSS or RStudio; APA-style empirical reporting

BENENTR211.name: Marketing & Consumer Engagement
BENENTR211.description2: This course unpacks what drives consumer engagement with brands and how marketers build customer trust responsibly. It introduces key marketing concepts, consumer psychology, AI/technology-driven marketing innovation, and brand and communication strategies. Students will explore real-life case studies, develop a strategic marketing plan and learn how marketers build sustainable brand strategies.
BENENTR211.profile: Connects marketing strategy and consumer psychology to responsible brand development and customer engagement. Students study strategic planning, customer experience, qualitative and quantitative insights, brand identity, digital marketing and behavioural framing. Applied projects analyze a company's strategy and response to disruption, design a brand, and investigate a consumer phenomenon using academic literature and primary and secondary evidence. Customer-journey mapping translates findings into recommendations.
BENENTR211.topics: Strategic marketing planning; Marketing mix; Customer centricity and experience; Consumer journeys; Market research and augmented insights; Brand identity and image; Brand partnerships; Digital and social marketing; Responsible marketing; Consumer psychology; Nudging and framing; Emerging technologies and marketing agility
BENENTR211.methods: Marketing-strategy case analysis; Advertising-campaign analysis; Kapferer brand-identity prism; Brand design; Primary and secondary consumer research; Consumer-journey mapping; Disruption-response planning

BENENTR312.name: International Business & Governance
BENENTR312.description2: This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business environment.
BENENTR312.profile: Examines how international trade, globalization and political, sociocultural and technological forces shape firms' cross-border decisions. Economic foundations include trade theories, foreign direct investment, foreign exchange and the monetary system. Students analyze governance, responsibility and trade-policy conflicts, investigate an international-business question, and develop an evidence-based market-entry strategy covering country attractiveness and business functions. A tariff case applies game theory to stakeholder choices and negotiation.
BENENTR312.topics: Globalization; International trade theories; Foreign direct investment; Foreign exchange and international monetary systems; Trade policy and economic integration; Cross-border governance; Corporate responsibility; Sociocultural and technological business environments; International business strategy; Market entry; Marketing, supply chains and human resources; Economic warfare
BENENTR312.methods: Trade-policy case analysis; Game-theoretic stakeholder analysis; Secondary-data analysis and visualization; Country and market-attractiveness assessment; Market-entry strategy development; Research-question formulation and evidence evaluation

BENENTR212.name: Strategy & Digital Transformation
BENENTR212.description2: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.
